certification.description: Voluntary Quality and Performance Specification. Unlike builders hardware or metal packaging containers which are under strict statutory Quality Control Orders (QCOs), industrial foundry binders and accessories under IS 10032 : 2013 are certified on a voluntary basis. Conforming manufacturers are eligible to apply for a BIS license to use the Standard Mark (ISI Mark) under Scheme-I of Schedule-II of the BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018. Compliance is routinely mandated inside public and private sector foundry, metallurgy, and heavy casting procurement tenders. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable to industrial foundry resin binders.
requirements: The organic binder must be supplied in a liquid state, typically formulated from furan resins (based on furfuryl alcohol), phenolic resins, or alkyd systems. The specific chemistry dictates the corresponding acid catalyst or hardener system required for room-temperature curing.
To ensure uniform pumpability and rapid, consistent mixing with sand grains, the viscosity must not exceed specified limits when tested via standard viscometers (such as Ford Cup viscometry at 30°C).
Prescribes a minimum percentage of non-volatile active resin solids to ensure that the binder provides sufficient dry strength after the carrier solvents evaporate.

For binders intended for steel or high-grade iron castings, the nitrogen content is strictly restricted. High nitrogen levels can decompose under casting temperatures and dissolve into the liquid steel, causing pinhole porosity and structural casting defects.

The binder system, when mixed with standard sand and catalyst, must provide a usable bench life (pot life) to allow core box packing, followed by a controlled strip time (setting time) after which the core gains sufficient green strength to be safely stripped.

The fully cured sand core must not evolve excessive gas when exposed to molten metal temperatures. Evolved gas volume must remain within restricted limits (such as 16 to 20 ml/g max) to prevent gas blowholes in castings.

All binders of the same grade, type, and batch manufactured under essentially similar conditions in a single day constitute one inspection lot. Random samples are selected for both physical sand-mix tests and wet chemical/referee analyses. Non-conforming lots must be isolated and rejected.

Foil stock must be supplied as continuous, solid cold-rolled coils, wound tightly with uniform tension to prevent telescoping or collapse of the inner core during transit and uncoiling.

Stock is typically supplied in one of the standard tempers as specified by the purchaser (such as O - Annealed or H14 - Half-hard) in accordance with temper standards to ensure appropriate starting ductility.

The surface must be clean, smooth, bright, and completely free from physical defects such as edge cracks, laminations, pinholes, slivers, deep scratch marks, corrosion, or heavy surface oxidation which could cause tearing or localized punctures during foil-rolling.

Wrought test specimens must satisfy mechanical limits (such as ultimate tensile strength and minimum elongation percentage) to ensure the sheet can sustain the severe tensions experienced in high-speed, downstream multi-stand rolling mills.

If any test specimen fails to comply with mechanical or chemical limits, a retest is permitted: two additional samples must be drawn from the same lot. The lot is accepted if both retests pass, and is rejected if either retest fails.

IS 10259 is not a primary product certification standard (not directly certified under a separate voluntary or mandatory license) but rather serves as the mandatory technical delivery, sampling, and inspection code referenced by downstream product standards. Any manufacturer producing aluminium corrugated sheets, wrought plates, or castings under mandatory or voluntary BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark) schemes (such as IS 1254, IS 737, or IS 617) must perform routine quality control, sampling, batch selection, defect reviews, retesting, and rust-proof packaging in strict accordance with IS 10259. requirements: General requirements relating to the supply, inspection, and verification of chemical/mechanical parameters of aluminium products must conform to the master framework of IS 10259.

Products must be smooth, clean, and completely free from harmful surface defects such as cracks, severe draw lines, lamination slivers, edge splitting, pitting, corrosion scale, or foreign inclusions that would compromise structural ductility or load capacity.

If any primary test specimen fails to meet chemical or mechanical properties during quality auditing, a strict retest protocol applies: a) Two additional test samples must be selected at random from the same lot; b) If both retests conform, the entire lot is deemed to have passed; c) If either retest specimen fails, the entire lot represented shall be rejected.

Materials of the same alloy designation, size, nominal thickness, and temper condition must be grouped together into a single control unit or lot (defined as up to 300 tubes, 1000 kg, or as specified by product codes) for statistical testing, ensuring traceable representation.

Samples must be prepared and analyzed per IS 504 parts or equivalent instrumental techniques (such as Spark Optical Emission Spectroscopy) to verify that heavy metals and alloy concentrations stay within specification boundaries.

Packaging methods must ensure full protection of the polished or rolled aluminium surfaces. The packing mode must prevent mechanical bending or denting and completely isolate the metals from moisture ingress to eliminate transit water staining or white rust corrosion.

All mechanical checks must be evaluated in the exact delivery temper or condition requested by the purchaser (such as O - Annealed, H14 - Half-hard, or T6 - Solution Treated and Artificially Aged) per IS 5052 temper designations.

The machining allowance is defined as the minimal thickness of extra metal (over-metal) left on the raw forging's outer envelope. This thickness must be sufficient to ensure that during subsequent material removal, all hot-rolling scale, decarburized surface layers, and surface micro-cracks are completely removed, leaving a pristine finished surface.

The forgings must be sound and free from piping, cracks, laminations, seams, deep laps, and slag inclusions. Visual and non-destructive testing (such as magnetic particle flaw detection per IS 3703) must verify surface soundness.

requirements: The flake resin must be synthetic in nature, produced by the catalytic reaction of phenol and formaldehyde, representing a novolak (novolac) type resin suitable for the hot coating of sand.

Sampling and physical testing must be carried out according to the manufacturer's production batches. A suitable sized sample must be drawn from all the drums of a particular batch, mixed thoroughly, and used for testing.

The physical dimensions of the resin flakes (length, width, and thickness in millimetres) are strictly specified under Table 1 of the standard to ensure uniform melting and distribution during hot coating.

A sand mix prepared with 3.5% flake resin on sand and 15% catalyst on flake resin must satisfy strict physical requirements specified under Table 1, including cold tensile strength, stick point, and gas content.
Each drum or bag of product must carry the name of the product, date of manufacture, expiry date, and the production batch number.
Conforming products may be marked with the ISI Certification Mark on their containers as a further assurance of quality.

certification.description: Voluntary Engineering Code of Practice. Since IS 11812:1986 is an engineering guideline rather than a direct manufacturing product, it does not carry a separate mandatory BIS license or ISI certification mark. However, its design rules, stress-relief practices, venting details, and dipping protocols are universally mandated inside all national public works (CPWD), power transmission (PGCIL), railways, and industrial structural steel engineering contracts to prevent on-site mechanical twisting and structural damage during the hot-dip galvanizing process.
requirements: All structural members used in an assembly should be pre-formed accurately to avoid SPRINGING ACTION and forced alignment during fit-up, thereby eliminating built-in mechanical tension that could be released in the zinc bath.

Where massive weldments or heavy clamping forces are involved, the fabricated assembly should be stress-relieved by a suitable low-temperature heat treatment prior to galvanizing to prevent thermal distortion.

Symmetrical cross-sections (such as I-beams, tubes, and pipes) are highly recommended because they distribute heating and cooling forces evenly about both axes. Non-symmetrical sections (such as channels, angles, or assemblies with dissimilar thicknesses) are highly prone to warping.
Corners on sheet metal products such as pans, bins, and containers should be fabricated with a generous radius to minimize localized stress concentration.

Tightly contacting or overlapping steel surfaces must be completely sealed by continuous welding. This prevents the entrapment of pickling acids or flux in crevices, which can cause severe interior rust, non-uniform coating, or build up explosive steam pressures at galvanizing temperatures (815–850°F / 435–455°C) that pose serious injury risks to plant personnel.

Riveting of fabricated parts prior to dipping is not recommended if the kettle size allows single-dip total immersion. Crevices at contacting rivet heads entrap pickling acids, leading to localized rusting.

If a sheet metal or fabricated structure is too large for single-dip kettles, the sheets and framing should be galvanized separately and assembled post-galvanizing using galvanized or aluminum alloy rivets.

Each fabricated article must be submerged with complete safety. Closed hollow shapes (including pipes, structural hollow sections, pressure vessels, footing stiffeners, and gussets) must be provided with clipped or drilled vent holes to prevent air pockets, ensure complete zinc coverage, and facilitate rapid zinc drainage.

Articles should be dipped in a manner that ensures uniform heating and cooling across their sections. Vertical dipping of channel profiles and framing is preferred over horizontal or low-angle immersion.

Slag and flux residues left by coated welding electrodes are chemically inert to standard pickling acids. All weld slag must be removed prior to pickling by chipping, wire brushing, or sand/shot blasting to prevent uncoated bare spots.

For pipe railings, handrails, and similar assemblies, joints must feature open-mitre configurations at all times to allow continuous internal venting and zinc flow. Closed or blind sections are strictly prohibited, and floor flanges should be made of cast or wrought steel instead of cast iron.

certification.description: Strict Statutory Mandatory Certification. Under the 'Copper Products (Quality Control) Order' (QCO) issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry (DPIIT), Government of India, all copper wire rods for electrical applications must conform to IS 12444:2020 and bear the mandatory BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark). Manufacturing, importing, distributing, or stocking non-certified copper wire rods is a punishable statutory offense under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016. Exemption is granted solely for export-oriented shipments. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable to industrial copper conductor feedstocks.
requirements: Each coil or packaged bundle of copper wire rods must bear the BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark) along with the manufacturer's registered licence number (CM/L) and standard reference to verify compliance.

Under Amendment No. 1, the standard specifies requirements for continuous cast copper wire rods with cross-sectional nominal diameters over 6 mm to 35 mm (originally capped at 18 mm). Tolerances on diameter and unit mass must stay within strictly bounded limits.

Electrolytic Tough Pitch (ETP Grade) wire rods must be made of electrolytically refined copper, demonstrating a minimum copper purity of 99.90 percent (Cu >= 99.90% min, including silver) and a nominal oxygen content restricted to a maximum of 400 ppm (O2 <= 400 ppm max). Sulphur limits have been modified under the revision.

Oxygen-Free Copper (OFC Grade) wire rods must be made of high-purity copper, demonstrating a minimum copper content of 99.95 percent (Cu >= 99.95% min) with Oxygen strictly limited to less than 10 ppm (O2 < 10 ppm max) to prevent cuprous oxide inclusion hazards.

Rods must ensure maximum electrical transport efficiency. Minimum electrical conductivity must be at least 100 percent or 101 percent (IACS) depending on grade, with a maximum electrical resistivity strictly capped at 0.01707 micro-ohm-meter at 20°C.

To guarantee that rods can withstand high-speed drawing down to extremely fine wires without snapping on downstream manufacturing lines, the rods must show high ductility: minimum tensile strength is typically 160 N/mm² or 210 N/mm² depending on the specific hard/annealed state, with a minimum elongation at break of 35 percent.

The surface of the continuously cast copper wire rods must be clean, smooth, uniform, and completely free from physical defects such as cracks, severe scratches, oxidation scale, flakes, or foreign inclusions.

To verify internal and mechanical soundness of the rod, a compression/upsetting test is conducted. Specimens of the rod are compressed axially to a specified fraction of their original height; the compressed piece must show zero visible cracking, splitting, or material delamination.

Specifically for the Oxygen-Free Copper (OFC) grade, a hydrogen embrittlement test must be performed. Specimens conditioned and heated in a hydrogen atmosphere must show zero micro-cracking or physical brittleness under subsequent bending, verifying that the copper is completely free from cuprous oxide inclusions.

For compliance auditing, standard physical test samples of 6 metres length and chemical drill samples of 100g (or 5 pieces of 5 cm length) must be selected at random from the control lots in accordance with IS 4905 randomization guidelines.

Under the 'Copper Products (Quality Control) Order' (QCO) issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry (DPIIT), Government of India, all copper tubes for plumbing must conform to IS 14810:2000 and carry the mandatory BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark). Enforcement began on October 19, 2024, for medium and large-scale enterprises, January 19, 2025, for small enterprises, and April 19, 2025, for micro enterprises. Manufacturing, importing, distributing, or stocking non-certified plumbing tubes is a punishable statutory offense under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable to industrial plumbing copper tubes.
requirements: Every commercial package or tube length of plumbing pipe must bear the BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark) along with the manufacturer's registered licence number (CM/L) and standard reference to verify compliance.

The tubes must be manufactured from Grade Cu-DHP (Phosphorized deoxidized copper with high residual phosphorus) conforming to IS 191 (Part 8), ensuring a minimum copper purity of 99.90 percent (including silver) and phosphorus content restricted to between 0.015 and 0.040 percent [1]. This composition prevents hydrogen embrittlement and maintains long-term structural toughness.

Plumbing tubes must be manufactured through a solid drawing process (seamless construction). Longitudinal welding is strictly prohibited to guarantee maximum pressure handling, leak tightness, and high resistance to splitting.

Tubes must be cut to size in coils or straight lengths, properly drafted, and securely sealed at both ends. This sealing prevents dirt, moisture, and microbial contaminants from entering the tube bore during transit and storage.

The inner and outer surfaces of the tubes must be clean, bright, smooth, and completely free from harmful defects such as deep scratches, cracks, inclusions, pitting, or visible oxidation scale, with the bore entirely free from deleterious residue films.

Every single tube length must withstand a standard hydrostatic test pressure calculated per formula: P = (2 * F * t) / (D - t)
where P is pressure (MPa), t is wall thickness (mm), D is outside diameter (mm), and F is design stress (72.5 MPa for HD, 60.0 MPa for HB, and 46.0 MPa for O condition). The tube must sustain this pressure for at least 5 seconds with zero leakage or sweating.

Consignments of identical diameters, thicknesses, and tempers are grouped into inspection lots of 300 tubes or 1,000 kg (whichever is greater). One random sample tube is tested per lot. If it fails, two retest tubes are drawn. If both retests pass, the lot is accepted; if either fails, the entire lot is rejected.

As an alternative to the standard hydrostatic pressure test, each tube must be tested to a minimum internal air pressure of 35 N/cm² (approximately 3.5 bar) for a minimum period of 5 seconds. The entire length of the tube must be immersed in water during testing, showing zero bubbles or signs of leakage.

For tubes supplied in Temper Annealed (TA) and Annealed (O) conditions only, longitudinal samples must show uniform and complete recrystallization when examined under a magnification of 75x per IS 4748. The average grain size must lie strictly between 0.010 mm and 0.050 mm, with the maximum grain size not exceeding 0.050 mm.

For TA and O condition tubes, by mutual agreement, a stress-corrosion test is conducted using ammonia vapor. A 150 mm length tube specimen is degreased, pickled in a 10% sulphuric acid solution, washed, and dried. It is suspended in a closed desiccator above an ammonium chloride solution adjusted to pH 10 using sodium hydroxide flakes. After 24 hours of exposure, it is pickled lightly and examined for any signs of cracking. Cracking at sawn ends is ignored.
Alternatively, a stress-corrosion test can be conducted in accordance with IS 2305 : 1988 using a mercurous nitrate solution. The specimen must show zero signs of chemical cracking.

One test must be conducted from each lot for: a) Tensile properties (tested per IS 2655); b) Hardness properties (Vickers tested per IS 1501); c) Flattening properties (tested per IS 2328); d) Drift expanding properties (tested per IS 2335) to verify wall ductility and flare capability without splitting.
The inner and outer surfaces of the tubes must be clean, bright, smooth, and completely free from harmful defects such as severe scratches, cracks, inclusions, pitting, or oxidation scale.

To prevent physical bending, rubbing, and surface damage during transport, the tubes must be suitably covered with polyethylene sheets and packed with proper plastic inserts at the ends. The gross weight of each packaging box must not exceed 1,000 kg, and the bottom of the packing cases must be completely rigid to maintain perfect straightness.

A lot comprises up to 300 tubes or 1,000 kg (whichever is higher) of the same grade, size, thickness, and condition. Ten tubes are drawn at random for visual/dimensional checks (zero defectives allowed). If the lot passes dimensions, one sample is tested for chemical, mechanical, flattening, and drift expanding tests, and one sample for microscopic examination.

Deposited weld metal must undergo radiographic inspection to verify soundness prior to mechanical testing. Test weld assemblies must be welded in the downhand position using a multi-run technique without post-weld heat treatment. Wire-flux combinations suitable for both AC and DC must be tested on AC.

Four transverse bend specimens (face and root bends) must be tested. The weldment satisfies the code if bent 120° over a former having a diameter equal to 3 times the specimen thickness, with zero cracks/defects exceeding 3 mm across or 1.5 mm along length.

Weldments must meet specified minimum impact energy values (e.g. 47 J for T31–T34). If the average of three specimens falls slightly below the threshold (between 34 J and 40 J), three additional specimens must be tested and added to the average. Machining or grinding away some of the good substrate material as well as the damaged surface to provide an adequate and uniform flat surface to accept the new thermal spray deposit. The ends of the undercut zone must be angled at 15° to 45° to the base metal (as shown in Fig. 1) to prevent notch effects or stress concentration.

Prior to roughening, all traces of oil, grease, paint, or other foreign contaminants must be completely removed from the undercut and adjacent surfaces. The undercut section must be roughened (such as by grit blasting) to ensure robust mechanical interlocking of the sprayed coating with the substrate.

Due to the low heat of combustion and low particle velocities of flame spray (both wire and powder) processes, both grit blasting and the application of an intermediate bond coating are usually required to ensure adequate bond strength.
For plasma spray processes, both surface roughening (via grit blasting) and the application of an intermediate bond coating are mandatory and essential to secure the coating.

Verification and certification of coating equipment must be performed either through regular calibration of process meters and pressure/flow gauges, or through demonstration of physical coating application, or a combination of both.

The effectiveness of the thermal spray coating depends heavily on final finishing. Finer grit grinding wheels must be used on dense, hard-to-penetrate coatings. Crucially, the coating must always be kept under compression during machining; grinding/cutting down through the sprayed surface towards the substrate minimizes delamination and particle pull-out.

Inspection must be performed after all finishing operations are complete. Both destructive (e.g. cross-section evaluation) and non-destructive (e.g. dye penetrant or ultrasonic) methods of evaluation may be utilized to verify bond integrity and thickness.

Extruded tube diameters and wall thicknesses must satisfy the strict limits of Table 2. Under Amendment No. 2, the eccentricity tolerance of the tube walls is calculated using the corrected mathematical formula: 1/2 (AA+BB) . (d)^2 (where d is the nominal wall thickness).

certification.description: Strict Statutory Mandatory Certification. Under the 'Aluminium and Aluminium Alloy Products (Quality Control) Order' (QCO) issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India, all notified aluminium products—including alloy forging stocks and hand/die forgings for structural applications—must comply with the applicable standard and bear the mandatory BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark). Manufacturing, importing, distributing, or selling non-certified structural alloy stocks is a statutory offense. Export-oriented fabrications conforming to foreign buyers' specifications are exempt. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable to aircraft structural alloy billets and forgings.
requirements: Each package or consignment of forging stock or forgings conforming to this standard must carry the BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark) along with the manufacturer's registered licence number (CM/L).

The forging alloy represents Al-Cu-Mg-Si-Mn composition (Alloy 24345) and must strictly meet chemical requirements: Aluminium (Remainder), Copper (3.9 to 5.0%), Silicon (0.5 to 1.2%), Manganese (0.4 to 1.2%), and Magnesium (0.2 to 0.8%).
Forging stock and forgings must be of uniform quality, sound, and entirely free from harmful structural or visual defects such as cracks, voids, laps, seams, folds, or non-metallic inclusions.
The forgings are typical solution heat-treated and precipitation-hardened (artificial aging) to develop optimal metallurgical strength and fatigue properties.

Extruded forging stock up to and including 10 mm thickness/diameter must develop: a) 0.2% Proof Stress: minimum 380 MPa; b) Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS): minimum 430 MPa; c) Elongation: minimum 9 percent.

Extruded forging stock over 10 mm and up to and including 20 mm must meet: a) 0.2% Proof Stress: minimum 400 MPa; b) Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS): minimum 430 MPa; c) Elongation: minimum 9 percent.

Extruded forging stock over 20 mm and up to and including 75 mm must meet: a) 0.2% Proof Stress: minimum 420 MPa; b) Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS): minimum 460 MPa; c) Elongation: minimum 9 percent.

Extruded forging stock over 75 mm and up to and including 150 mm must meet: a) 0.2% Proof Stress: minimum 390 MPa; b) Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS): minimum 430 MPa; c) Elongation: minimum 9 percent.

Extruded forging stock over 150 mm and up to and including 200 mm must meet: a) 0.2% Proof Stress: minimum 350 MPa; b) Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS): minimum 400 MPa; c) Elongation: minimum 9 percent.

Forgings of all sizes prepared from cast billets, hot-rolled plates, or extruded stocks must develop: a) 0.2% Proof Stress: minimum 395 MPa; b) Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS): minimum 420 MPa; c) Elongation: minimum 6 percent.

Even if the material satisfies chemical and mechanical tension tests, it must be rejected if faults in manufacturing are detected or if dimensional tolerances, hardness, and metallurgical structures do not comply.

Unless otherwise agreed, each package for dispatch must contain only one size, alloy, and temper of material, and must be permanently marked with the batch/lot number, manufacture date, grade (Alloy 24345), and the manufacturer's trademark.
